topics.title: Types of solutions
topics.summary: What a solution is, which component is the solvent, and the nine ways a solute and a solvent can combine.

lessons.title: What a solution is, and its nine types
lessons.objective: Define a solution, identify the solvent and solute in an example, and classify a solution by the physical states of its components.

blocks.text: A **solution** is a ==homogeneous mixture of two or more components==. Homogeneous means the composition and properties are the same everywhere in the sample - a drop from the top of a glass of sugar water tastes exactly like a drop from the bottom.

The component present in the largest amount is usually the **solvent**; it decides the physical state of the solution. The other components are **solutes**. This unit deals only with **binary solutions** (two components).

blocks.title: At the level of particles
blocks.text: In a solution the solute is spread out as single molecules or ions among the solvent particles. That is why it looks uniform even under a microscope, and why it does not settle on standing.

blocks.title: Why composition matters
blocks.text: Composition changes properties sharply. NCERT's examples: brass (Cu + Zn), German silver (Cu + Zn + Ni) and bronze (Cu + Sn) behave differently; 1 ppm of fluoride in water prevents tooth decay, 1.5 ppm mottles teeth, and much more is poisonous; injections must match the ion concentrations of blood plasma.

blocks.text: **How to classify:** first decide the solvent (it gives the solution its state), then the state of the solute. Hydrogen in palladium is a solid solution (palladium is solid) with a gaseous solute.
NCERT Exercise 1.2 asks for *a solid solution in which the solute is a gas*: the answer is **hydrogen in palladium**. The amalgam of mercury with sodium is the liquid-in-solid example.

items: A solution is a homogeneous mixture; the solvent sets its physical state.
Nine types: three solvent states × three solute states (NCERT Table 1.1).
Hydrogen in palladium = gas in solid; sodium amalgam = liquid in solid.

topics.title: Expressing concentration of solutions
topics.summary: Seven ways to say how much solute is present, when each is used, and which ones change with temperature.

lessons.title: Percentages and parts per million
lessons.objective: Calculate mass %, volume %, mass by volume % and ppm, and choose the right one for a situation.

blocks.text: 'Dilute' and 'concentrated' are qualitative words. Calculations need a number, and the right number depends on the job: industry uses mass %, pharmacy uses mass/volume %, pollution data uses ppm, vapour pressure uses mole fraction, and colligative properties use molality or molarity.

blocks.title: The idea behind every percentage
blocks.text: A percentage compares a **part** with the **whole** and scales the answer to 'out of 100'. In mass % both part and whole are masses, so the units cancel and the result has no unit. ppm is the same idea scaled to 'out of a million', which suits tiny amounts.

blocks.label: (i) Mass percentage (w/w)
blocks.tex: ext{Mass \% of a component} =  rac{	ext{mass of the component in the solution}}{	ext{total mass of the solution}} 	imes 100
blocks.where: 10% glucose by mass = 10 g glucose in 90 g water (100 g of solution). Commercial bleach is 3.62% sodium hypochlorite by mass.
blocks.conditions: Both masses in the same unit. The bottom line is the **solution** (solute + solvent), not the solvent.

blocks.label: (ii) Volume percentage (V/V)
blocks.tex: ext{Volume \% of a component} =  rac{	ext{volume of the component}}{	ext{total volume of the solution}} 	imes 100
blocks.where: 10% ethanol (V/V) = 10 mL ethanol made up to 100 mL. A 35% (V/V) ethylene glycol antifreeze lowers the freezing point of water to 255.4 K (−17.6 °C).
blocks.conditions: Used for liquids dissolved in liquids. Volumes are not always additive, so 'made up to 100 mL' is the precise wording.

blocks.text: **(iii) Mass by volume percentage (w/V)** is the mass of solute in grams dissolved in **100 mL of solution**. It is common in medicine and pharmacy - normal saline is 0.9% (w/V) NaCl.

blocks.label: (iv) Parts per million (ppm)
blocks.tex: ext{ppm} =  rac{	ext{number of parts of the component}}{	ext{total number of parts of all components}} 	imes 10^6
blocks.where: Used for trace amounts. A litre of sea water (1030 g) holds about $6 	imes 10^{-3}$ g of dissolved O$_2$, i.e. 5.8 g per $10^6$ g = 5.8 ppm. Like percentages, ppm can be mass/mass, volume/volume or mass/volume.

blocks.title: Mass percentage of glucose
blocks.problem: 15 g of glucose is dissolved in 135 g of water. Find the mass percentage of glucose.
blocks.relation: Mass % = (mass of component ÷ mass of solution) × 100.
blocks.why: The question asks what part of the whole solution's mass is glucose.

convert.t: Mass of solution = 15 g + 135 g = 150 g
convert.why: The denominator is the **solution**, so add the solute to the solvent first.

calc.why: Grams cancel, so a percentage has no unit.

blocks.check: 15 g is one-tenth of 150 g, so 10% is right. Dividing by 135 instead would give 11.1% - the classic slip.

items: Percentages and ppm compare part to whole: divide by the **solution**.
w/V % = grams of solute per 100 mL of solution.
ppm = part ÷ whole × $10^6$, for trace amounts.
blocks.next: Lesson 2.2: mole fraction - counting particles instead of grams.

lessons.title: Mole fraction
lessons.objective: Calculate the mole fraction of each component from masses, and explain why it has no unit and why the fractions add to 1.

blocks.text: Grams do not tell you how many particles there are: 1 g of hydrogen contains far more molecules than 1 g of chloroform. **Mole fraction** counts particles instead. It answers: out of every mole of particles in the mixture, what fraction belongs to this component?

blocks.title: Why chemists like it
blocks.text: Many properties depend on **how many** particles are present, not how heavy they are. Vapour pressure (lesson 4) is one: the solvent's share of the surface depends on its share of the particles, so Raoult's law is written with mole fractions.

blocks.label: (v) Mole fraction
blocks.tex: x_A =  rac{n_A}{n_A + n_B}, \qquad x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_i = 1
blocks.where: No units. It is the natural measure for vapour pressure (Raoult's law) and gas mixtures.
blocks.conditions: The denominator is the **total** moles of every component. For a two-component solution $x_B = 1 - x_A$.

blocks.title: Mole fraction from mass %
blocks.problem: Find the mole fraction of ethylene glycol ($\ce{C2H6O2}$) in a solution that is 20% $\ce{C2H6O2}$ by mass.
blocks.relation: $x_{	ext{glycol}} = n_{	ext{glycol}}/(n_{	ext{glycol}} + n_{	ext{water}})$
blocks.why: Mole fraction needs **moles** of both components, but the question gives only a percentage by mass.

convert.t: Take 100 g of solution: 20 g glycol and 100 − 20 = 80 g water.
convert.why: **Why 100 g?** A percentage is 'per 100 g', so choosing 100 g turns 20% straight into 20 g. Any mass would give the same mole fraction - 100 g just makes the arithmetic easy.

calc.why: Mass ÷ molar mass turns grams into moles.
Keep four figures until the last step, then round.

blocks.check: Glycol is a minority component, so a small value (well below 0.5) makes sense; the two fractions add to 1.

board.t: In 100 g solution: glycol 20 g, water 80 g

items: Mole fraction = moles of a component ÷ total moles. No unit.
All mole fractions add to 1.
From a mass %, take 100 g of solution, then turn each mass into moles.

lessons.title: Molarity and dilution
lessons.objective: Calculate molarity from a mass and a volume, explain every step (including where 40 g mol$^{-1}$ and 0.450 L come from), and use $M_1V_1 = M_2V_2$ for dilution.

blocks.text: **Molarity** tells you how many moles of solute there are in each litre of the **solution**. If a bottle says 0.25 M NaOH, every litre of that solution contains 0.25 mol of NaOH, and every 100 mL contains one-tenth of that.

blocks.title: Why the volume of the solution?
blocks.text: In the laboratory you dissolve the solute and then add water **up to a mark** on a volumetric flask. The volume you know is the final volume of the whole solution, not the volume of water you added - so molarity is defined per litre of solution.

blocks.label: (vi) Molarity
blocks.tex: ext{Molarity} =  rac{n_{	ext{solute}}}{V_{	ext{solution}}\ (	ext{in L})}
symbols: volume of the solution (not the solvent)
blocks.where: Units mol L$^{-1}$ (= M = mol dm$^{-3}$). 0.25 M NaOH has 0.25 mol NaOH in 1 L of solution.
blocks.conditions: Volume in litres. Because the volume changes slightly with temperature, molarity does too.

blocks.text: Two different M's appear in the next example. **M** after a number (0.278 M) is the unit 'molar' = mol L$^{-1}$. **M** in $n = m/M$ is the molar mass in g mol$^{-1}$. Lower-case **m** is mass in grams - and later in the chapter, molality. Read the units to tell them apart.

blocks.title: Molarity of an NaOH solution - every step explained
blocks.problem: Calculate the molarity of a solution containing 5 g of NaOH in 450 mL of solution.
blocks.find: Molarity of the solution, in mol L$^{-1}$.
blocks.relation: Molarity = moles of solute ÷ volume of solution in litres.
blocks.why: Molarity is defined in **moles** per **litre**. The question gives a mass in grams and a volume in millilitres, so both must be converted before we can divide.

convert.t: Molar mass of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g mol$^{-1}$
convert.why: One formula unit of NaOH has one Na, one O and one H atom, so add their atomic masses. This means **40 g of NaOH is exactly 1 mol**.
**Why divide 5 by 40?** If 40 g make one mole, then 5 g is 5/40 of a mole. The grams cancel and leave mol.
Molarity is per **litre**, and 1 L = 1000 mL, so divide the millilitres by 1000.

calc.why: We divide by the **final volume of the solution**, because molarity asks how much solute there is in each litre of the whole solution.

blocks.check: Sense check: 0.125 mol in a bit less than half a litre should give a bit more than 0.25 mol per litre - and 0.278 is a bit more than 0.25. Units: mol ÷ L = mol L$^{-1}$.

board.t: Molar mass of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g mol$^{-1}$

blocks.boardNote: In the exam, write the formula, the substitution with units, and the answer with its unit. The explanations above are for understanding; you do not need to write them.

blocks.text: Dilution: same solute, more solution
Adding water changes the volume but not the number of moles of solute. Since moles = molarity × volume, the product $MV$ is the same before and after.

blocks.label: Dilution
blocks.conditions: Holds exactly when only solvent is added, because the moles of solute do not change. $V_2$ is the **final** volume of the solution. $V_1$ and $V_2$ may be in mL as long as both are in the same unit.

blocks.prompt: 5 g of NaOH is in 450 mL of solution. If water is added until the volume is 900 mL, what happens to the molarity?

blocks.text: Dilution keeps the moles of solute fixed: $M_1V_1 = M_2V_2$. NCERT Intext 1.3(b): 30 mL of 0.5 M $\ce{H2SO4}$ diluted to 500 mL gives $0.5 	imes 30/500 = 0.03$ M.

items: Molarity = moles of solute ÷ litres of **solution**.
Turn grams into moles with the molar mass, and mL into L by dividing by 1000.
Dilution: moles stay the same, so $M_1V_1 = M_2V_2$.

lessons.title: Molality, and which units change with temperature
lessons.objective: Calculate molality using the solvent's mass in kilograms, and explain why molarity changes with temperature while molality, mole fraction and mass % do not.

blocks.text: **Molality** counts moles of solute for every kilogram of **solvent**. It is the measure used for boiling-point elevation and freezing-point depression later in this chapter.

blocks.title: Why a mass and not a volume?
blocks.text: When a liquid is heated it expands, so the same solution takes up more litres - its molarity falls a little even though nothing has been added. Mass does not change with temperature. Molality uses only masses (moles come from masses too), so it stays constant whatever the temperature.

blocks.label: (vii) Molality
blocks.tex: m =  rac{n_{	ext{solute}}}{W_{	ext{solvent}}\ (	ext{in kg})}
blocks.where: Units mol kg$^{-1}$. 1.00 m KCl = 1 mol (74.5 g) KCl dissolved in **1 kg of water** (solvent, not solution).
blocks.conditions: Divide by the solvent's mass in **kilograms**, not by the solution's mass.

blocks.title: Molality of ethanoic acid in benzene
blocks.problem: Find the molality of a solution of 2.5 g of ethanoic acid ($\ce{CH3COOH}$) in 75 g of benzene.
blocks.relation: $m$ = moles of solute ÷ mass of solvent in kg.
blocks.why: Molality is moles per kilogram of **solvent**; we have grams of solute and grams of solvent, so convert both.

convert.why: **Why the solvent's mass?** Molality is defined per kilogram of solvent. Adding the 2.5 g of acid (77.5 g) would be the solution's mass - a common mistake.

blocks.check: 0.042 mol in less than a tenth of a kilogram should give roughly half a mole per kilogram - it does.

left.title: Do not change with temperature
items: Mass %
ppm (mass)
Mole fraction
Molality

right.title: Change with temperature
items: Molarity (NCERT's example)
Any measure that uses the volume of the solution, such as mass by volume %
Reason: volume expands or contracts with temperature; mass does not.

blocks.text: A 2023 assertion-reason item: 'Molarity of a solution in liquid state changes with temperature' because 'the volume of a solution changes with change in temperature'. Both true, and the reason explains the assertion (option A).

blocks.title: When are molarity and molality nearly equal?

blocks.text: For a **dilute aqueous** solution, 1 L of solution is almost 1 kg of water (the solute adds little mass and volume, and water's density is close to 1 g mL$^{-1}$). Then molarity and molality are nearly the same number, and questions sometimes treat them as equal.

This is an approximation. It fails for concentrated solutions or other solvents: 20% aqueous KI (NCERT Intext 1.5) is 1.51 mol kg$^{-1}$ but 1.45 mol L$^{-1}$. If a question gives molarity and a formula needs molality, use the approximation only when the solution is dilute and aqueous, and say so.

items: Molality = moles of solute ÷ kg of **solvent**.
Mass-based measures (mass %, ppm, mole fraction, molality) do not change with temperature; volume-based ones (molarity, w/V %) do.
For dilute aqueous solutions molarity ≈ molality, but only approximately.

lessons.title: Converting between concentration units
lessons.objective: Starting from a mass % and a density, find the molality, molarity and mole fraction of the same solution, explaining each choice.

blocks.text: Board questions often give one kind of concentration and ask for another. The trick is always the same: pick a convenient amount of solution, find the mass of solute and of solvent, and convert from there.
Converting between units - the method that always works

blocks.title: Given mass % and density, find molality, molarity and mole fraction
items: Assume **100 g of solution**. Mass of solute = the percentage; mass of solvent = 100 minus that.
Molality = (moles of solute) / (mass of solvent in kg).
Volume of solution = 100 g / density (in g mL$^{-1}$) - convert to litres. Molarity = moles of solute / that volume.
Mole fraction = moles of solute / (moles of solute + moles of solvent).

blocks.title: One solution, three concentrations
blocks.problem: An aqueous NaOH solution is 10% NaOH by mass and has a density of 1.10 g mL$^{-1}$. Find its molality, molarity and the mole fraction of NaOH. (NaOH = 40, H$_2$O = 18 g mol$^{-1}$)
given: Molar masses: NaOH 40, water 18 g mol$^{-1}$
blocks.relation: $m = n/W_{	ext{solvent}}$;  Molarity $= n/V_{	ext{solution}}$;  $x = n_{	ext{NaOH}}/(n_{	ext{NaOH}} + n_{	ext{water}})$
blocks.why: All three need the moles of NaOH; molality also needs the solvent's mass, molarity the solution's volume, and mole fraction the moles of water.

convert.t: Take 100 g of solution: 10 g NaOH and 90 g water.
convert.why: A 100 g basis turns '10%' directly into 10 g.
Density links the solution's mass (100 g) to its volume, which molarity needs.

blocks.check: Molality and molarity come out close but not equal - the solution is fairly concentrated, so 1 L of it is not 1 kg of water. Mole fraction is small because water molecules far outnumber NaOH units.

board.t: In 100 g solution: NaOH = 10 g = 0.25 mol; water = 90 g = 5.0 mol

blocks.text: Molality divides by the mass of the **solvent**; molarity divides by the volume of the **solution**. Using the solution's mass in molality is the most common error in this topic.

items: Choose 100 g of solution when a mass % is given.
Solvent mass → molality; solution volume (from density) → molarity; moles of both → mole fraction.
Keep extra digits until the final answer.

questions.q: A 500 g sample of lake water contains 0.004 g of dissolved oxygen. Express the oxygen content in ppm (by mass).

scaffold.t: ppm = (mass of O$_2$ ÷ mass of sample) × $10^6$
Mass of sample = 500 g (the oxygen's mass is negligible in comparison)

mistakes.msg: That is the mass percentage (× 100). ppm multiplies by $10^6$.
You found the fraction but did not multiply by $10^6$.

hints: Which measure is used for tiny amounts, and what is it 'out of'?
Divide 0.004 by 500, then multiply by one million.

questions.q: 16 g of methanol ($\ce{CH3OH}$, 32 g mol$^{-1}$) is mixed with 36 g of water. Find the mole fraction of methanol.

mistakes.msg: 0.5 ÷ 2 compares methanol with water only. The denominator is the **total** moles: 0.5 + 2.
That is the mole fraction of **water**. The question asks for methanol.
16 ÷ 52 is a mass fraction. Mole fraction uses moles.

hints: Mole fraction needs moles of both components.
Water: 36 ÷ 18 = 2 mol. Now divide methanol's moles by the total.

questions.q: 5.85 g of NaCl is dissolved in water and the solution is made up to 500 mL. Find its molarity. (Na = 23, Cl = 35.5)

scaffold.t: Molar mass of NaCl = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 g mol$^{-1}$

mistakes.msg: Check the volume: it must be in **litres** (500 mL = 0.500 L), not millilitres.
You divided the volume by the moles. Molarity = moles ÷ litres.
You used the mass in grams instead of moles. Divide the moles (0.100 mol) by the volume.

hints: Molarity needs moles of solute and litres of solution. You already have the moles.

questions.q: 3.0 g of urea ($\ce{NH2CONH2}$, 60 g mol$^{-1}$) is dissolved in 250 g of water. Find the molality.

mistakes.msg: Check whether you converted the solvent mass to kilograms: 250 g = 0.250 kg.
You divided by the solution's mass (253 g). Molality uses the **solvent** only: 250 g.
You divided the mass of urea, not its moles. Use 0.050 mol.

hints: Molality = moles of solute ÷ kg of solvent. Which mass is the solvent?

questions.q: 4.5 g of glucose ($\ce{C6H12O6}$) is dissolved in 100 g of water. Find the molality of the solution. (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)

mistakes.msg: Check whether you converted the solvent mass to kilograms: 100 g = 0.100 kg.
You divided by the solution's mass (104.5 g). Molality uses the solvent only.
You divided the mass of glucose (not its moles) by the kilograms of water. Convert grams to moles first.

hints: You need moles of glucose and kilograms of water.
Molar mass of glucose = 6(12) + 12(1) + 6(16) = 180 g mol$^{-1}$.

teach.relation: $m$ = moles of solute ÷ kg of solvent
teach.why: Molality is defined per kilogram of solvent.

questions.q: An aqueous urea solution is 6% urea by mass. Find its molality. (Urea = 60 g mol$^{-1}$)

scaffold.t: Take 100 g of solution: 6 g urea and 94 g water.

mistakes.msg: You divided by 0.100 kg - the solution's mass. Molality uses the solvent: 94 g = 0.094 kg.
Check whether you converted the solvent mass to kilograms: 94 g = 0.094 kg.

hints: Which mass goes in the denominator of molality?
